question: What are the two major jobs of the human ear?
explanation: You got this! The ear does more than just let you hear your favorite music; it also contains the balance system that keeps you steady and upright. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T2#GNS211_U4_T2_h1)

question: Which type of sensory receptors inside the ear pick up sound and movement?
explanation: Think 'mechanical'! Mechanoreceptors respond to physical forces like sound waves and fluid movement in the ear. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T2#GNS211_U4_T2_h1)

question: What is the everyday medical name for the outer, visible part of the ear?
explanation: Great job! The auricle (or pinna) is shaped just right to catch sounds and funnel them down into the ear canal. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T2#GNS211_U4_T2_h2)

question: What substance do the glands in your ear canal secrete to trap dust and bugs?
explanation: Cerumen is just the medical term for earwax! It acts as a natural shield protecting your delicate ear canal from dirt and bacteria. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T2#GNS211_U4_T2_h2)

question: Which tiny bone in the middle ear is attached directly to the eardrum?
explanation: The malleus (also known as the hammer) rests right against the eardrum to catch its first vibrations. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T2#GNS211_U4_T2_h3)

question: Why is your Eustachian tube so important?

options.C: Equalizing air pressure in the middle ear

explanation: Ever felt your ears 'pop' when swallowing or yawning? That is your Eustachian tube balancing out air pressure so your eardrum stays comfortable. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T2#GNS211_U4_T2_h3)

question: Which snail-shaped structure in the inner ear handles hearing?
explanation: Spot on! The cochlea is packed with fluid and tiny cells that turn sound vibrations into messages your brain can understand. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T2#GNS211_U4_T2_h4)

question: What do we call the tiny hair-like structures inside the ear that bend to trigger nerve signals?
explanation: Stereocilia sit proudly on top of hair cells. When inner ear fluid moves, these little hairs bend and kick off electrical signals to the brain. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T2#GNS211_U4_T2_h4)

question: What happens right after sound waves make your eardrum vibrate?

options.A: Cerumen is pushed out of the external canal
options.B: The auricle changes shape to capture more sound
options.C: The Eustachian tube opens to release excess air
options.D: The auditory ossicles move and amplify the vibration

explanation: The three tiny bones (malleus, incus, stapes) spring into action, boosting the sound vibrations before passing them deeper into the ear. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T2#GNS211_U4_T2_h5)

question: If a patient's stapes bone becomes fused and stuck, where does sound transmission get blocked first?

options.A: Equalizing pressure through the Eustachian tube
options.B: Capturing sound waves in the external auricle
options.C: Secreting cerumen inside the ear canal
options.D: Transferring vibrations to the oval window of the internal ear

explanation: Since the stapes normally acts like a piston pushing against the oval window, a stuck bone stops that crucial transfer of energy dead in its tracks. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T2#GNS211_U4_T2_h5)

question: What tiny calcium stones help your brain sense gravity and straight-line movement?
explanation: Think of otoliths as tiny natural 'ear stones' that shift with gravity over sensory cells, letting you know if you are standing up straight or leaning. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T2#GNS211_U4_T2_h6)

question: Which inner ear structure detects when you spin or turn your head?
explanation: You've got this! The three semicircular canals sit at different angles to catch motion whenever you turn your head in any direction. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T2#GNS211_U4_T2_h6)

question: Which cranial nerve carries hearing and balance messages from the ear to the brain?
explanation: Cranial nerve VIII is also known as the vestibulocochlear nerve—combining balance (vestibule) and hearing (cochlea) into one pathway! [learn more](GNS211_U4_T2#GNS211_U4_T2_h7)

question: Which lobe of the brain processes the sounds you hear?
explanation: The temporal lobe houses your auditory cortex, turning nerve signals from your ears into clear, recognizable sounds. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T2#GNS211_U4_T2_h7)

question: What is the main reason behind conduction deafness?

options.A: Destruction of hair cells from loud music
options.B: Blocked transmission of sound waves to the inner ear
options.C: Damage to the auditory cortex in the brain

explanation: Conduction deafness simply means a physical block—like earwax, fluid, or a stuck bone—is stopping sound waves from traveling smoothly inside. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T2#GNS211_U4_T2_h8)

question: What medical term describes a constant ringing or buzzing sound in the ears?
explanation: Tinnitus is a very common issue where a person hears phantom sounds like ringing or buzzing when no external sound is actually there. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T2#GNS211_U4_T2_h8)
